Chip stocks pared losses Thursday after concerns over debt-heavy balance sheets triggered a broader AI-driven sell-off on Wall Street. title: Nvidia Stocks Fall 3.0% With Cash Conversion in Focus After Baird's Warning - TradingView
content: Nvidia, the AI-computing supplier NVDA, faces sharper scrutiny over financing the AI boom, with shares trading at $214.63, down 3.0%, at 9:47 a.m. ET on October 15. In a Yahoo Finance interview, Baird strategist Ted Mortonson questioned chipmakers' growing financing role. That puts cash collection in focus. Selling more chips drives earnings. Collecting the money determines how much cash those earnings deliver. Nvidia's August 26 results show the gap: second-quarter operating cash flow reached $24.077 billion against $59.688 billion in net income, a conversion rate of roughly 40.3%. Rising accounts receivable absorbed $22.346 billion, while the cash-flow reconciliation removed $7.771 billion in equity-security gains from earnings. Those are different moving parts. Receivables reflect money owed by customers; investment gains do not represent cash collected from chip sales. The GF Score graphic shows 95/100, with strong profitability and growth but a visibly weaker GF Value readingan impressive business can still carry a demanding valuation. The cash figures alone establish neither troubled collections nor improper revenue recognition. The next test is whether customer payments catch up with sales. Stronger collections would reinforce the earnings story. Further cash tied up in receivables would make payment terms and customer credit quality harder for investors to overlook. title: Jensen Huang Says Nvidia Must Work With Chinese AI Firms - TradingView
content: Nvidia NVDA CEO Jensen Huang said the chipmaker must work with Chinese AI companies to monitor the risks of a technology he called potentially dangerous, CNBC reported. We absolutely should work with each other so that we advance the technology safely, Huang said at a media briefing in London. Nvidia shares were down 1.90% intraday as of 11:00 a.m. ET. Huang said he already holds discussions with many researchers in China and wants more of them. He said the U.S. should step up that dialogue and that he had urged the U.K. to do the same, describing Britain as well placed to host such talks. That stance puts him at odds with OpenAI's Sam Altman and Anthropic's Dario Amodei, who have called for greater regulation. Governments in both countries are moving in a similar direction. In September, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent discussed a possible U.S.-China AI dialogue with his Chinese counterpart, He Lifeng, including a channel for incidents up to a national security level. A Chinese readout of the Trump-Xi meeting cited Xi as saying the two sides could keep talking about AI's risks and benefits and work together to prevent misuse. title: Volvo expands partnerships with NVIDIA on automated driving - TradingView
content: Volvo Cars VLVLY is expanding its decade-long partnership with NVIDIA NVDA to develop advanced automated-driving technology designed to improve safety and enable more effortless journeys in future vehicles. The Swedish automaker said on Thursday that the collaboration will combine its vehicle-safety systems and engineering expertise with NVIDIA’s NVDA artificial intelligence and accelerated-computing technologies. The system is intended to help future Volvo VLVLY models navigate complex driving environments, including highways, crowded urban roads and parking areas. The technology will make its debut in a next-generation Volvo VLVLY model as part of what the company described as its largest-ever product push. The expanded partnership will incorporate NVIDIA’s NVDA Hyperion sensor and computing architecture, Halos operating system and Alpamayo Stack driving software. Volvo VLVLY said the initiative aims to establish a new benchmark for automated driving, with features gradually enabling eyes-off and mind-off driving. The companies are building on a collaboration that began in 2017, as Volvo VLVLY prepares to integrate more advanced computing capabilities into its next generation of electric vehicles. Volvo VLVLY Chief Executive Officer Håkan Samuelsson said the partnership combines the automaker’s longstanding safety expertise with NVIDIA’s NVDA artificial intelligence technology to develop safer and more appealing vehicles. NVIDIA NVDA Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang said the collaboration would bring together Volvo’s VLVLY safety systems and NVIDIA’s computing platforms to make driving safer and less demanding for customers. The companies said their shared focus is to deliver automated-driving technology that is safe, convenient and worthy of consumer trust. title: Micron vs. NVIDIA: Which AI Stock Is the Better Buy After Earnings? - TradingView
content: Semiconductor behemoths Micron Technology MU and NVIDIA Corporation NVDA benefited from the artificial intelligence (AI) boom. With strong growth and an upbeat outlook, both seem poised to capitalize on rising AI infrastructure demand. But which stock offers a better buying opportunity? Let’s explore – Micron’s AI Growth and Expanding Margins Boost Outlook As AI infrastructure needs high-performance memory, demand for Micron’s cutting-edge high-bandwidth memory (“HBM”) chips has surged. This momentum helped the company post revenues of $54.23 billion in the fiscal fourth quarter of 2026, up sharply from $11.32 billion a year ago, according to its Sept. 30 press release. For fiscal 2026, Micron’s revenues were $133.19 billion, up from $37.38 billion in fiscal 2025. Its guidance remains even more encouraging, with the company expecting revenues of $61.5 billion, plus or minus $1.5 billion, in the first quarter of fiscal 2027. The data center business continues to be Micron’s key growth engine, benefiting from an increase in AI-related demand. Additionally, Micron’s profit margins are reaching exceptional levels. Its non-GAAP gross margin increased from 84.9% in the fiscal third quarter of 2026 to 87% in the fiscal fourth quarter, supported by higher selling prices, a favorable product mix, and operating leverage. Further, the company’s management expects its Strategic Customer Agreements to improve earnings visibility. NVIDIA’s AI Demand Fuels Revenue Growth and Strong Profitability According to NVIDIA’s Aug. 26 press release, the company’s revenues climbed 106% year over year and 18% sequentially to $96 billion in the fiscal second quarter of 2027. Its Data Center segment remained the primary growth driver, with revenues surging 117% year over year to $89 billion. Going forward, NVIDIA expects revenues of $108 billion, plus or minus 2%, in the fiscal third quarter of 2027, signaling further sequential growth. The company also expects profitability to remain strong as its Vera Rubin platform has entered the full production stage, while NVIDIA remains well-positioned to capitalize on the next wave of AI infrastructure demand. By the way, NVIDIA’s gross margin rose to 75% in the fiscal second quarter of 2027 from 72.4% a year earlier, while both GAAP and non-GAAP net income increased. NVIDIA’s GAAP operating income more than doubled year over year, implying strong operating leverage. Micron or NVIDIA: Which AI Stock to Buy After Earnings Both Micron and NVIDIA’s recent strong revenue growth, expanding margins, and upbeat guidance could boost both stocks. However, U.S. chip export restrictions to China and stiff competition could limit NVIDIA’s further growth, while Micron’s evolution from a highly cyclical memory stock to a vital supplier of AI infrastructure could drive sustained growth. Moreover, NVIDIA’s debt-to-equity ratio of 14.1% exceeds Micron’s 3.3%, indicating greater financial leverage and potentially greater downside risk during economic downturns. Therefore, Micron’s evolving role in AI infrastructure and lower financial leverage make it a more compelling buy than NVIDIA. Additionally, Micron appears more attractively valued than NVIDIA. Per the price/earnings ratio, MU trades at 5.18 forward earnings compared with NVDA’s forward earnings multiple of 23.93. Micron currently has a Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy). title: Nvidia-backed drug discovery firm Iambic climbs on trading debut - TradingView
content: Iambic Therapeutics IAM, a life sciences company backed by Nvidia NVDA and AbbVie ABBV, among others, rose more than 10% above its initial public offering price on Thursday in its first trading session as a listed firm. Iambic IAM shares opened at $16.15 at about 12 pm ET, roughly unchanged from the IPO price, then quickly added about 11% to reach $17.95 about an hour later, implying a valuation of roughly $876M. Late Wednesday, the San Diego-based AI-driven drug discovery firm priced the offering of roughly 9.4M shares at $16.00, targeting about $150M in gross proceeds. A 30-day option was available for underwriters to purchase up to ~1.4M shares additionally at the IPO price adjusted for underwriting discounts and commissions. Iambic IAM expects the offering to generate about $135M in net proceeds, which it intends to use, among other things, to advance its lead asset IAM1363. The oral tyrosine kinase inhibitor is currently undergoing a Phase 1/1b clinical trial for advanced HER2-altered solid tumors ahead of a potentially registrational study expected to begin next year. Since its inception in 2019, the company has raised approximately $461.8M from technology- and healthcare-focused investors, including Nvidia NVDA. ARK Investment Management, one of its existing investors, and Duquesne Family Office LLC had agreed to buy $60M worth of stock at the offering price, a filing indicated last week. Nvidia (NVDA) CEO Jensen Huang addressed the recent discord at key partner and fallen AI stock darling CoreWeave (CRWV) on Thursday, expressing optimism in the data center operator following a 15% rout on Wednesday and a smaller dip on Thursday morning. "CoreWeave's strength is improving every day," Huang shared at a Bloomberg event in Stockholm. "I'm optimistic. Their cost of capital is actually decreasing." His input was much anticipated this week as concerns about the health of CoreWeave and its exposures to Nvidia have continued to build. Huang's need to weigh in wasn't a surprise to veteran tech analyst Tal Liani, who just this morning published a bullish note on CoreWeave with an aggressive $140 price target. "Don't forget that Nvidia is basically financing all these deals with them, with other hyperscalers because they want to block off the competition. They want to make sure that CoreWeave and others are using Nvidia GPUs and not AMD GPUs," Liani said on Sozzi Unleashed. Liani added, "So at the end of the day, there is an inherent interest both ways. And I'm sure that you're going to hear from everyone on the planet that has a vested interest in the build-out of data centers. You're going to hear comforting kinds of comments about the validity of the demand and the sustainability of the demand, including Jensen. It's just a question of time." CoreWeave's corporate bonds across maturities have continued to be dumped amid fears of an AI slowdown and its implications for the company's precarious balance sheet. This price reflects trading activity during the overnight session on the Blue Ocean ATS, available 8 PM to 4 AM ET, Sunday through Thursday, when regular markets are closed. The selling spread to other AI cloud stocks: Nebius (NBIS) fell 11%, Oracle (ORCL) dropped another 9%, and the following stocks sank more than 10%: DigitalOcean (DOCN), Hut 8 (HUT), Cipher (CIFR), TeraWulf (WULF), and IREN (IREN). Nvidia's own stock fell 2% Thursday morning. In January of this year, Nvidia announced an expansion of its relationship with CoreWeave. The deal included Nvidia investing $2 billion in CoreWeave stock. CoreWeave committed to using Nvidia's technology to build more than 5 gigawatts of AI factories by 2030. Nvidia now holds 47.2 million shares of CoreWeave stock, or around 10% of the company. CoreWeave buys GPUs from Nvidia and then rents that compute out to other companies, including hyperscalers like Meta (META). Semiconductor and memory chip stocks extended their losing streak on Thursday as concerns over mounting debt and rising financing costs for artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure projects continued to weigh on the sector. Nvidia (NVDA) fell over 2%, Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) dropped 4%, while Micron Technology (MU) and SanDisk (SNDK) slipped roughly 4% and 6%, respectively, extending losses from earlier in the week. See what 10M+ investors are talking about. Get the Stocktwits Daily Rip for what retail is watching right now, free to your inbox In a Thursday note, Saxo Bank Chief Investment Strategist Charu Chanana said there was insufficient evidence of a systemic AI credit crisis, even as investors increasingly questioned the sustainability of the financing model behind the infrastructure boom. However, Chanana warned that financing pressures in the AI infrastructure industry could eventually affect semiconductor suppliers if companies are forced to scale back investment. The bank noted that infrastructure providers depend on financing and large customer contracts to fund expansion, while equipment suppliers rely on those customers continuing to build capacity. If rising borrowing costs force infrastructure operators to moderate spending, Saxo said the impact could spread beyond chipmakers to industrial equipment, power infrastructure and construction companies. Saxo pointed to AI cloud provider CoreWeave (CRWV), where yields on some bonds have approached 15%. Elevated bond yields do not necessarily signal an imminent default. However, repricing of CoreWeave's debt suggests that investors are becoming less willing to finance AI infrastructure growth at any cost, the note stated. The selling continued despite Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. (TSMC) reporting a strong quarter. The chip manufacturer's fiscal third-quarter (Q3) revenue rose 51% to NT$1.49 trillion, beating market forecasts. In dollar terms, sales rose 41%. Early Thursday, TSM forecast fourth-quarter revenue would rise up to 61% from a year ago, after posting its sixth consecutive quarter of record earnings. According to the Saxo strategist, strong demand is no longer enough to sustain elevated stock valuations, with investors increasingly scrutinizing profitability, financing costs and returns on investment. Chanana pointed to strong operating performance across the semiconductor industry, including Micron's revenue growth, ASML's higher sales outlook and TSMC's September revenue increase. The focus is shifting toward whether companies can translate strong demand into sustainable cash flow and earnings growth, rather than simply announcing larger infrastructure investments, the note said. title: Zesty Launches Automated Fractional GPUs, Bringing Automation to NVIDIA CUDA-Native GPU Fractioning - Yahoo Finance UK
content: Tip: Try a valid symbol or a specific company name for relevant results Following NVIDIA's open-source release of the Run:ai platform, Zesty's new autonomous capability continuously adapts GPU memory allocation, compute sharing, and workloads placement as demand changes, enabling more workloads to run on each GPU. SAN MATEO, Calif., Oct. 15, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Zesty, a leader in Kubernetes optimization, today announced support for NVIDIA's CUDA-native GPU fractioning. Following NVIDIA's open-source release of Run:ai as part of the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform, Zesty's Automated Fractional GPUs adds the autonomous layer that continuously decides GPU memory allocations and compute sharing modes, as well as steers workload placement as AI workload demand fluctuates. With these autonomous capabilities, teams can improve GPU utilization, run more workloads on existing infrastructure, reduce the need for excess GPU capacity, and lower infrastructure costs while protecting application performance. 66% of organizations hosting generative AI models run some or all of their inference on Kubernetes, and GPU capacity for those workloads is expensive and often constrained. Teams have traditionally allocated entire GPUs to individual workloads or shared them using time-slicing, NVIDIA Multi-Process Service (MPS), or NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU (MIG), which divides each GPU into fixed hardware-based partitions. Allocations cannot keep pace with dynamic AI workloads and real-time changes in demand. As a result, GPU memory and compute end up stranded, and teams buy more GPUs even while existing capacity sits unused. NVIDIA's recent open-source release of Run:ai brings CUDA-native GPU fractioning to Kubernetes through the GPU Fractioning Operator, which enforces per-workload GPU memory limits and works with Kubernetes schedulers. The fractioning mechanism makes flexibility possible and defines how workloads can divide a GPU but does not determine how to allocate that capacity. Deciding which workloads share each GPU, how much memory each one receives, and how those allocations should change as demand rises and falls requires a separate decision layer. Zesty provides that layer. Its Automated Fractional GPU capability continuously determines which workloads should share each GPU, how many can safely run together, how much GPU memory each one receives, which sharing mode fits each workload, and when those allocations should increase or decrease. Decisions draw on actual GPU memory usage and utilization, observed workload behavior over time, and the latency requirements and resource limits defined by teams beforehand. Every change stays within the performance and availability policies teams set for each workload. "GPUs are among the most expensive and constrained resources infrastructure teams manage today. They're difficult to secure, costly to add, and shared by AI workloads whose needs change constantly. Now NVIDIA has opened GPU fractioning to the ecosystem, and Zesty is making their allocation intelligent and autonomous," said Pini Ben Nahum, VP R&D at Zesty. "Autonomous GPU Resource Management adjusts GPU memory and compute sharing while guiding workload placement as each workload's needs rise and fall. Teams can pack more onto existing hardware, reducing new GPU purchases and the cost of running AI in production without giving up performance quality." The capability deploys as a lightweight agent in the Kubernetes cluster and works alongside NVIDIA Run:ai GPU Fractioning Operator and the Kubernetes scheduler, supporting both time-slicing and MPS. It requires no application code or model changes, and installation does not restart running workloads. On a supported GPU stack, Zesty manages the Kubernetes configuration needed for optimization without manual manifest changes. Automated Fractional GPUs is available today as part of the Zesty platform. To learn more, visit http://zesty.co/platform/automated-fractional-gpus. About ZestyZesty helps organizations reduce infrastructure costs through autonomous resource optimization. The platform continuously matches resources to real-time workload demand, automatically eliminating overprovisioning and improving infrastructure efficiency while protecting application performance. By replacing constant manual rightsizing and resource tuning with policy-driven automation, Zesty enables teams to run leaner Kubernetes environments without adding operational risk. With Automated Fractional GPUs, Zesty is extending this same approach to GPU infrastructure, helping teams get more from existing GPU capacity while controlling the growing cost of AI workloads. Founded in 2019, Zesty is focused on making infrastructure more efficient, automated, and cost-effective. In its latest report, JPMorgan noted that, with U.S. inflation data coming in higher than expected and tech stocks continuing to adjust, U.S. retail investors' risk appetite has noticeably weakened. Zhitong Finance APP learned that on Thursday, JPMorgan noted in its latest "Retail Investor Watch" report that, with U.S. inflation data coming in higher than expected and tech stocks continuing to adjust, retail investors' risk appetite has noticeably weakened. During the week of October 8–14, net retail buying totaled just $3.4 billion, far below the 12-month average of $6.7 billion per week. However, despite the overall weakening of retail buying, certain leading AI and semiconductor stocks remain popular; NVIDIA (NVDA.US), in particular, saw approximately $942 million in net purchases over the week. JPMorgan's strategy team, led by Arun Jain, noted that the brief rebound in retail investor enthusiasm has failed to sustain. With no positive catalysts and subdued market risk sentiment, retail inflows have slowed further. The report shows that last week, overall retail inflow intensity was at only the 5th percentile of its historical distribution, indicating extremely weak buying pressure. Specifically, ETF inflow intensity fell to the 2nd percentile, while individual stock trading remained at the 21st percentile. On Wednesday, the U.S. September Consumer Price Index (CPI) further weighed on market sentiment. JPMorgan noted that the overall CPI rose about 0.65% month-over-month and 3.7% year-over-year in September, with the month-over-month increase exceeding market expectations by the largest margin since March 2024. Core CPI climbed roughly 0.33% month-over-month and 2.6% year-over-year, indicating that inflationary pressures remain persistent. As a result, the Nasdaq 100 index fell by about 2% on Wednesday, and the S&P 500 also ended its streak of several consecutive trading days without a single-day decline of more than 1%. JPMorgan economists expect the core personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index to rise 0.31% month-over-month and 3.1% year-over-year in September. The bank believes this inflation level is sufficient to make a Fed rate hike in October a viable option; however, its baseline forecast remains that the Fed will raise rates again in December. Retail investors are pulling out of tech ETFs but continue to selectively buy individual semiconductor stocks. Technology stocks have been the sector most visibly affected by recent shifts in retail investor behavior. The report notes that, with the semiconductor sector posting a roughly 9% decline over the past week, the capital that had previously flowed back into technology ETFs has swiftly reversed course. JPMorgan data show that retail investors' fund-flow indicator for technology ETFs plummeted from the 73rd percentile in the previous week to the 4th percentile, signaling a shift from aggressive buying to pronounced selling. Among them, the Direxion Daily Semiconductor 3x Bull ETF (SOXL.US) and the iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX.US) were the primary targets of selling. Meanwhile, momentum‑strategy ETFs have also seen outflows, with the iShares MSCI USA Momentum Factor ETF (MTUM.US) being one of the main drag factors. JPMorgan notes that since October, the momentum factor has continued to weaken, primarily because long positions heavily weighted toward speculative growth stocks and semiconductor shares have underperformed short positions dominated by software stocks. However, in contrast to the sell-off hitting technology ETFs, retail investors continue to show strong buying interest in certain individual tech stocks. Data show that last week, net retail inflows into ETFs totaled $3.2 billion, while net purchases of individual stocks amounted to just $200 million, underscoring that investors overall still prefer allocating capital through ETFs. At the individual stock level, the technology sector is one of the few areas that has seen net inflows of capital. Aside from the "Big Seven" U.S. stocks, retail investors have also been heavily buying shares in certain semiconductor, memory‑chip, and AI‑infrastructure–related companies. Among them, NVIDIA became the stock most favored by retail investors, with net purchases totaling $942 million for the week. Alphabet (GOOGL.US), Tesla (TSLA.US), Apple (AAPL.US), Amazon (AMZN.US), and Meta (META.US) received approximately $132 million, $111 million, $74 million, $53 million, and $39 million in net purchases, respectively. By contrast, Microsoft (MSFT.US) saw net selling by retail investors totaling about $15 million. Among other tech stocks, SanDisk (SNDK.US) recorded net buying of approximately $238 million, while Broadcom (AVGO.US) saw net buying of roughly $139 million. Retail investors' choices within the semiconductor sector have clearly diverged. Micron Technology (MU.US) saw net sales of approximately $123 million, while AMD (AMD.US) recorded net sales of about $70 million, indicating that retail investors are not engaging in indiscriminate bargain-hunting across the entire semiconductor sector. JPMorgan noted that retail investors have recently reverted to their previous trading pattern—selling software stocks while selectively buying semiconductor and hardware stocks after pullbacks. This allocation strategy differs somewhat from the broader trend in institutional investors' holdings. Notably, despite recent corrections in tech stocks that have weighed on retail investors, portfolios remain relatively outperforming year-to-date, thanks to investors' early‑May buildup in semiconductor and memory‑chip equities and a subsequent shift toward hyperscale cloud‑computing companies following strong second‑quarter earnings reports from major tech firms. Financials, industrials, and consumer sectors were sold off, with capital further concentrating in AI leaders. Apart from technology stocks, retail investors have generally adopted a cautious stance toward other major sectors. According to JPMorgan data, last week saw net outflows of approximately $330 million from the financial sector, about $302 million from the industrial sector, roughly $240 million from the consumer discretionary sector, and around $186 million from the healthcare sector. The utilities sector has also been under sustained retail selling pressure since mid-to-late August, while industrial stocks have faced further selling pressure following the start of the third-quarter earnings season. From a thematic investment perspective, retail investors continue to concentrate their capital on AI data centers, electrification, tech giants, growth stocks, and equities tied to the commercialization of AI, underscoring that AI remains a key investment theme driving retail investor flows. However, the divergence in capital flows suggests that retail investors' approach to AI investing has shifted from the earlier widespread chasing of rising stocks to a more cautious, stock-specific screening process. JPMorgan is optimistic about semiconductor earnings reports, with Broadcom and Marvell remaining its top picks. As the third-quarter earnings season of 2026 unfolds, JPMorgan believes the semiconductor industry will be the market's main focus. The bank expects that, over the next seven days, 62 S&P 500 constituent companies will report their results, collectively accounting for approximately 14% of the index's total market capitalization, with a strong concentration in the financial and industrial sectors. For the semiconductor industry, JPMorgan maintains a cautiously optimistic outlook, expecting that most covered companies are still likely to deliver solid results and provide positive forward guidance, continuing the trend of both earnings and guidance exceeding expectations over the past few quarters. However, the firm emphasized that market attention in the semiconductor sector is shifting from the strength of demand to supply constraints—specifically, when capacity bottlenecks in areas such as advanced‑node foundry services and memory chips will ease, and when newly added capacity can effectively meet demand. In stock selection, JPMorgan continues to rank Broadcom (AVGO.US) and Marvell Technology (MRVL.US) as its top picks in the semiconductor sector, while also keeping an eye on NVIDIA, AMD, Micron Technology, and SanDisk. The firm believes that companies with AI‑related business exposure, benefiting from supply constraints, possessing strong pricing power, or poised to capitalize on the industry's cyclical recovery are more likely to see their earnings forecasts revised upward. In addition, JPMorgan specifically highlighted the latest performance of lithography equipment giant ASML Holding. ASML Holding's third-quarter gross margin reached 57.5%, exceeding its prior guidance, and its fourth-quarter guidance for sales, gross margin, and EBIT also surpassed market expectations. JPMorgan noted that the midpoint of ASML's 2026 growth guidance implies a growth rate of approximately 36%, higher than the firm's forecast of about 31% for the global wafer fabrication equipment market, suggesting the company is poised to continue outpacing the industry as a whole. More notably, ASML Holding has recently secured orders that exceed the capacity it can fully meet between 2027 and 2028; accordingly, the company is considering increasing its 2028 capacity expansion to more than approximately 30% above its previously planned level. title: Jensen Huang Is Giving $250 Million to AI Safety and Says He’d Cut Off Reckless Customers - 24/7 Wall St.
content: Jensen Huang just pledged a quarter-billion dollars to AI safety research and said he would cut off a customer building dangerous AI, but his own statements reveal how much wiggle room that threat actually contains. The company that sells the hardware behind the AI boom is now paying for research into whether that boom is safe, and its chief executive says he would walk away from a buyer who built something dangerous. On Wednesday, October 14, 2026, in London, Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA | NVDA Price Prediction) chief executive Jensen Huang presented a five-year compute donation for United Kingdom AI safety and security research, valued at $250 million. In an interview the same day, he said he would cut off a customer building dangerous AI. That creates a real tension for shareholders, because Nvidia’s revenue depends on customers deploying AI as fast as they can, and safety rules are among the forces that can slow deployment. The stock closed at $221.30, down 3.16%, then slipped 1.54% to $217.89 after hours. The decline came in a broad chip selloff driven by hot inflation data, and it has no visible link to Huang’s remarks. For a company with a market value of $5.34 trillion, the donation is financially insignificant, and its significance lies in what it signals about Nvidia’s priorities. The gift is computing time on Nvidia hardware, priced by Nvidia itself and paid for by the company. Nvidia said it will deliver $50 million in compute access annually through United Kingdom-based cloud partners. Most of that access goes to the wider UK research community, with a portion for Oxford’s BOLD lab, the SOFAIR lab led by UCL, and Imperial College London. Nvidia did not disclose what the program actually costs it. Giving access to your own product also seeds something a cash grant would not: researchers who build their safety tools on your platform. Huang said, “AI capability and safety must advance together.” Asked whether he would cut off an irresponsible developer, he answered, “It’s a hypothetical, but yes.” He then attached conditions: “Before you do so, you would have a conversation. We don’t run other people’s companies.” He also called Nvidia’s technology general-purpose and said the current level of worry about AI is not warranted. Taken together, those statements leave the cutoff remark as an answer to a hypothetical, with no defined trigger or policy behind it. UK AI Minister Kanishka Narayan called the commitment “a vote of confidence in our world-leading strength and expertise in AI research.” That reaction points to the commercial return: Britain is still deciding how it will govern AI, so goodwill with the officials writing those rules, ties to top researchers, and a base of scientists trained on Nvidia software are worth more than the compute given away. This is strategy, and the research can still be valuable on its own terms. Nvidia generated $21.341 billion in free cash flow in its latest quarter alone, so the donation changes nothing about earnings or demand. Management guided third-quarter fiscal 2027 revenue to $108.0 billion. The pressure point is financing. Huang said in August that frontier research labs “are growing faster than what their balance sheets and credit profiles can support,” and Nvidia has stepped in with investments and credit support. CoreWeave (NASDAQ:CRWV) shares fell on worries about AI debt the same day, and deployment rules arriving faster than the next product cycle would be the second risk. The evidence points toward the bullish case. The safety pledge is a low-cost political investment that leaves demand untouched, and the inflation-driven drop puts the stock below the $237.47 it reached a week earlier. At about 45 times trailing earnings, the valuation assumes growth continues, which $279 billion in supply commitments supports. The view fails if financing stress spreads from CoreWeave to the frontier research labs Nvidia backs. Nvidia (NVDA) CEO Jensen Huang is unlikely to ignore the building pressure on CoreWeave's (CRWV) stock price and bond values. The simple reason is that he can't look the other way, given how intertwined Nvidia is with the most well-known — and debated — neocloud. First, in January of this year, Nvidia announced an expansion of its relationship with CoreWeave. The deal included Nvidia investing $2 billion in CoreWeave stock. CoreWeave committed to using Nvidia's technology to build more than 5 gigawatts of AI factories by 2030. Nvidia now holds 47.2 million shares of CoreWeave stock, or around 10% of the company. Second, CoreWeave is a huge customer of Nvidia, as shown in the chart below from the team at Boring Business. CoreWeave buys GPUs from Nvidia and then rents that compute out to other companies, including hyperscalers like Meta (META). "0% chance $NVDA lets $CRWV falter," tech analyst Daniel Newman said on X. Yet, CoreWeave's failure is what the market is chatting about. CoreWeave stock plunged 6% in premarket trading on Thursday following a 15% rout on Wednesday. "In our view, the company's long-term business model remains economically challenged; we maintain our Underperform," Bernstein analyst Madison Rezaei said in a note Thursday. Read more: Why CoreWeave stock may still rise over 100% despite financing fears, analyst says This price reflects trading activity during the overnight session on the Blue Ocean ATS, available 8 PM to 4 AM ET, Sunday through Thursday, when regular markets are closed. Two factors collided to spark Wednesday's sell-off. One, CoreWeave's corporate bonds across maturities continued to be dumped amid fears of an AI slowdown and its implications for the company's precarious balance sheet. The rise in yields on CoreWeave's bonds even spurred Elon Musk to post "Yikes" on X in response to a post by venture capitalist Chamath Palihapitiya. The selling spread to other AI cloud stocks: Nebius (NBIS) fell 11%, Oracle (ORCL) dropped another 9%, and the following stocks sank more than 10%: DigitalOcean (DOCN), Hut 8 (HUT), Cipher (CIFR), TeraWulf (WULF), and IREN (IREN). Read more: Why CoreWeave stock may still rise over 100% despite financing fears, analyst says Two, Gartner, in a new report, forecast that by 2030 "cost pressure and a lack of a differentiating business model will force over 80% of neocloud providers to cease independent operations." CoreWeave is a neocloud. The report essentially was akin to yelling "fire" in a crowded theater. At some point soon, Nvidia's Huang may have to step in and comment on Nvidia's confidence in CoreWeave. He has a financial interest in doing so, not only from an Nvidia standpoint, but also from the viewpoint of the wider AI boom his company's chips are fueling. title: History Says Nvidia Stock Usually Rises in the Fourth Quarter -- It Has in 20 of the Last 27 - The Motley Fool
content: Two of the seven down years erased over half the stock's value. What went wrong? Shares of Nvidia (NVDA -1.84%) hit another record on Tuesday, Oct. 6, closing at $239.24. If history's any guide, the October-to-December quarter has usually been a good one for the artificial intelligence (AI) chip giant's stock. Measured from the end of September to the end of December, Nvidia's shares rose in 20 of the 27 years from 1999 through 2025. The median change for all 27 fourth quarters was a gain of around 14%. But the record comes with two caveats. Nvidia's stock has climbed in most quarters during this stretch, not just the last one of the year. From 2000 through 2025, for example, it also gained in 20 of 26 first quarters. And two of the seven fourth quarters that went wrong cost shareholders over half their money. I think the calendar matters much less here than the report Nvidia puts out in the middle of it. Nvidia's fiscal year ends in late January, so its fiscal third quarter closes in late October. The report for that period tends to come in mid-to-late November, about halfway through the calendar fourth quarter. That report also gives management's revenue outlook for the fiscal fourth quarter, which runs roughly from November through January. Sure, even a great report doesn't promise a good quarter. Nvidia's fiscal third-quarter 2026 results, released Nov. 19, 2025, showed revenue up 62% year over year to $57.0 billion. Management also guided for $65.0 billion in the next quarter. The stock dropped around 3% a day later. It closed the fourth quarter down 0.04% -- a paper-thin loss in a quarter when the Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC +0.08%) gained around 3%. Nvidia's two worst fourth quarters broke the pattern for very different reasons. In 2000, the stock lost 60% as the dot-com crash pulled down tech stocks broadly. The Nasdaq Composite slid by around a third during the same three months. But Nvidia's shares were back above their late-September 2000 price by April 2001. The 2018 decline was mainly Nvidia's own problem, and the November report made it far worse. By report day, shares had already fallen about 28% from their late-September close. For the three months ended Oct. 28, 2018 (Nvidia's fiscal third quarter of 2019), revenue grew 21% year over year to $3.18 billion. But management forecast fiscal fourth-quarter revenue of $2.70 billion, around 15% below what the company had just reported. "Our near-term results reflect excess channel inventory post the cryptocurrency boom, which will be corrected," CEO Jensen Huang said in the earnings release. Put simply, too many of Nvidia's chips sat unsold with distributors and retailers after demand from cryptocurrency miners cooled. Shares fell about 19% the day after the report and ended the quarter down 52%, versus a loss of about 18% for the Nasdaq. They didn't climb back above their late-September 2018 close till February 2020. Notably, most of Nvidia's down fourth quarters lined up with a falling market. The Nasdaq fell in five of the seven. Only in 2020 and last year did Nvidia's shares drop while the index gained. Nvidia's business now looks nothing like it did in late 2018. For its fiscal second quarter of 2027 (which ended on July 26, 2026), revenue more than doubled, climbing 106% year over year to $96.2 billion. Management's forecast calls for $108.0 billion in fiscal Q3, plus or minus 2%. That's the bar the fiscal third-quarter report needs to clear. Meeting the guide would mean growth of about 89% from the $57.0 billion Nvidia reported a year earlier, a step down from 106%. The forecast for the following quarter could matter even more to the stock than the quarter itself. Nvidia's shares sell for around 15 times the consensus earnings estimate for fiscal 2028 (the year ending January 2028). Broadcom, another AI chipmaker, costs about 19 times its consensus earnings estimate for its next fiscal year. True, a price-to-earnings ratio is only as good as the estimates behind it. But at that price, Nvidia's shares could arguably weather a weaker report than the past few. So, does the calendar make Nvidia stock a buy right now? Not on its own. Twenty up years out of 27 mainly reflect a stock that's climbed in most quarters, whatever the season. And the worst years that broke the pattern saw a falling market, a weak forecast from Nvidia, or both. At today's price, I'd consider buying shares for the growth Nvidia is delivering. The fourth quarter's history doesn't do much for that case. Daniel Sparks and his clients do not have positions in any of the stocks mentioned. If you're looking for a company that's benefiting from the massive spending on artificial intelligence (AI), it's hard to go wrong with Nvidia (NVDA -1.84%) or Broadcom (AVGO -0.56%). Both are making a fortune selling the technology needed to build and operate AI data centers. And with major technology companies continuing to pour money into AI infrastructure, there's reason to believe both stocks have plenty of room to grow. But if I could own only one of these companies for the next five years, I'd choose Nvidia. That's why I continue to hold my shares. Broadcom has built an outstanding business around custom AI processors and networking equipment. But Nvidia has a few advantages that I believe make it the better long-term investment. There's something remarkable about Nvidia's growth. Despite becoming the world's most valuable company, the chipmaker is still posting revenue growth that would be impressive for a business a fraction of its size. Its fiscal 2027 second-quarter results showed revenue jumping 106% from a year ago to $96.2 billion, while net income increased 126% to $59.7 billion. Its data center business alone generated $89 billion in revenue, up 117%. And Nvidia expects another big quarter. Management projected fiscal third-quarter revenue of $108 billion, plus or minus 2%. "The surge in AI demand is driving a global infrastructure build-out, supported by an expanding and diverse set of growth opportunities, spanning hyperscalers, AI labs, AI natives, enterprises, and sovereign customers," Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress said. "We expect to grow revenue by approximately 70% in fiscal 2028." Nvidia's competitive advantage goes well beyond its graphics processing units (GPUs), which are used to train and run AI models. The company has built an entire computing platform around its processors, including networking equipment, software, and systems designed to work together. Its CUDA software platform also gives developers tools to build applications that run on Nvidia's hardware. And its Vera Rubin computing platform is already moving into production, giving Nvidia another opportunity to sell more powerful systems to its customers. Nvidia also generates enormous amounts of cash that it can use to develop new products, invest in AI companies, and reward shareholders. The company returned $26 billion to shareholders through repurchases and dividends in its latest quarter. Broadcom has nothing to hang its head over. The company carved out a valuable position in the AI market by designing custom processors, known as application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs). ASICs are tailored to the tasks they need to handle. The chips may not be as powerful or flexible as Nvidia's GPUs, but they can be just as efficient for specific tasks and are more affordable. That's appealing to major cloud providers that are spending billions on AI infrastructure. Broadcom also supplies networking technology that connects processors and other equipment inside data centers. As AI systems become larger, moving information efficiently between chips becomes increasingly important. The financial results show just how successful Broadcom has become. In its fiscal 2026 third quarter, Broadcom reported revenue of $29.6 billion, an increase of 86% from a year ago. The company generated $13.7 billion in free cash flow, giving it substantial resources to invest in its business and return money to shareholders. Management also projected fourth-quarter revenue of approximately $34.8 billion, representing 93% year-over-year growth. I wouldn't be surprised if both companies deliver strong returns over the next five years. Broadcom's custom chip business has significant potential, particularly as major technology companies seek alternatives to Nvidia's processors. But I think Nvidia has a stronger competitive position. Its GPUs are critical to the AI build-out, and its software, networking equipment, and complete systems give customers ample reasons to stay amid an increasingly competitive environment. If I'm choosing just one AI stock to hold through 2031, Nvidia gets my money. Patrick Sanders has positions in Nvidia. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Broadcom and Nvidia. Coinbase pays us for certain activity generated through this link. Prices displayed are informational. The financial markets are currently gripped by a singular obsession: artificial intelligence. This manic focus has pushed sector leaders like Nvidia (NVDA) to staggering heights, with its valuation crossroad vaulting past the $5 trillion mark. Driven by seemingly insatiable infrastructure demand from cloud titans, investors are treating NVDA as a surefire bet. Yet, beneath this euphoria lies a dangerous market asymmetry. As capital aggressively crowds into a handful of priced-to-perfection tech giants, exceptional value is being left behind in the wreckage of neglected sectors. While the market gladly pays extreme multiples for future AI promises, it is completely ignoring cash-generating machines hiding in plain sight—such as dating app pioneer Bumble (BMBL), which recently traded at a microscopic 2 times free cash flow. My name is Inan Dogan. I am Insider Monkey's cofounder and research director. I publish my personal stock picks in Insider Monkey's monthly premium newsletters. In February I finally pulled the trigger and added Bumble (BMBL) to our monthly newsletter's portfolio. Bumble was trading at 2 times free cash flow at the time. Its stock price was $2.75 at the time. I summarized my thesis as follows: "Bumble (BMBL) is currently significantly undervalued, trading at a "deep value" entry point following its massive post-IPO correction. I believe that the company's strong brand moat and high free cash flow generation provide a coiled-spring setup for a 300-400% recovery as management successfully executes its turnaround over the next few years. Bumble's stock price is finally cheap enough to provide an asymmetric risk-return opportunity. We don't know the exact figures for the entire 2025, but BMBL generated $182 million in free cash flow during the first 3 quarters. The total figure should be around $240 million. In late 2025, Bumble made a strategic move to purchase all outstanding TRA rights for $186 million in cash. While this was a significant one-time cash outlay, it eliminated a long-term liability and is expected to significantly improve the company's future cash flow profile by removing annual payment obligations. As of September 30, 2025, Bumble held $307.9 million in cash and equivalents against $589.4 million in total debt. If we add $60 million in free cash flow in Q4 and subtract the $186 million cash payment, we arrive at a total cash position of around $180 million. This means BMBL's net debt is around $410 million at the end of 2026. Basically we are buying the entire company (including its debt) at 3-4 times its cash flow." Today, Bumble disclosed that Ithaca Holdings will pay $6.05 per share. This is another Insider Monkey stock pick that more than doubled within a year (in this case 8 months). A year ago, I added Teva Pharmaceutical (TEVA) to our portfolio at $20. That stock is trading at $41 right now. We exited TEVA after an 80% gain earlier this year. We usually add one stock to our portfolio every month, so it isn't like we are picking dozens of stocks and BMBL and TEVA are cherry picked. Don't get me wrong. I believe AI is the most transformative technology ever. It is bigger than the industrial revolution and a large portion of our newsletter's portfolio is AI stocks, but not overpriced AI stocks. For example, there is an AI stock in our portfolio that is almost universally hated. Everyone hated BMBL which is why the stock was trading at two times free cash flow. This AI stock is so deeply unloved that you can currently buy it for less than the combined value of its cash and short-term investments. This is not some fringe player, either; it is a legitimate competitor with a real shot at winning its target market. If it succeeds, the stock has the potential to deliver a 10x return, if not more. Conversely, even if the company fails to capture the market, the downside is highly protected. Because the stock trades below the value of its cash and investments, it is still likely to deliver positive returns over time. It is a rare, asymmetrical win-win situation—yet mainstream investors continue to despise it just as they did Bumble. That's where the value is in the stock market. The current macro environment presents an incredible opportunity for stock-pickers willing to look away from the AI glare. Chasing Nvidia at a multi-trillion-dollar valuation requires believing that the AI capex cycle will never top out. Buying a cash-flowing asset like Bumble at a rock-bottom multiple requires only a belief that human beings will keep interacting, and that cash flow still matters. Ultimately, the market will remember how to weigh cash over hype. When it does, the real winners won't be those who bought the most expensive stocks on earth, but those who bought the most mispriced ones. Before moving on, I want to emphasize that Ithaca Holdings is stealing this company at $6.05 per share. Even at this price, they are paying just 5 to 6 times cash flow and will likely take the company public again in a few years at twice its current valuation. Therefore, do not make the mistake of thinking they are overpaying for the stock. Furthermore, I want to clarify that I am not shorting NVDA or holding a negative position against it. If the company manages to maintain its market dominance, the stock could easily post annual gains of 10% to 20% over the next couple of years. However, don't be surprised if NVDA eventually experiences a valuation contraction and trades down to 10 times its earnings. Almost all of NVDA's major clients are actively trying to develop proprietary versions of these chips to replace them—but that is a topic for another article. NVIDIA claims Vera Rubin can deliver 10 times the agent throughput of its previous Grace Blackwell platform at scale. Its production network spans more than 350 factories across 30 countries. The growth opportunity is substantial. In the second quarter of fiscal 2027, NVIDIA's revenues increased 106% year over year to $96.2 billion, while Data Center revenues climbed 117% to $89 billion. Management expects third-quarter revenues of $108 billion, plus or minus 2%, and anticipates Vera Rubin will contribute about 20% of Data Center revenues in the quarter. Major cloud providers, including CoreWeave, Alphabet, Microsoft, Oracle and Nebius, are preparing to deploy the platform. These partnerships could help NVIDIA capture demand for AI agents that perform multi-step tasks, increasing the need for computing power. Vera Rubin strengthens NVIDIA's growth outlook. However, supply constraints could limit its ability to meet demand, while rising memory costs could pressure margins. Management expects supply to remain a bottleneck through at least fiscal 2028. Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. AMD is challenging NVIDIA with its Instinct GPUs and Helios rack-scale systems. AMD's second-quarter 2026 revenues rose 50% year over year to $11.54 billion, while Data Center sales jumped 107% to $6.72 billion. Advanced Micro Devices also plans to supply up to 2 gigawatts of MI450 GPUs to Anthropic, with the first deployment expected in the first half of 2027. This could make AMD a stronger alternative as customers seek more AI computing capacity. Intel Corporation INTC is also expanding its data-center business. Its second-quarter 2026 revenues rose 25% year over year to $16.13 billion, supported by demand for its processor products. Intel is investing in its CPU, advanced packaging and manufacturing capabilities to capture more AI infrastructure spending. However, NVIDIA's integrated GPU systems, networking and software ecosystem remain important advantages. Advanced Micro Devices' upcoming MI450 platform and Intel's processor business offer customers more choices. Still, NVIDIA's Vera Rubin ramp could help it maintain its lead if it delivers the promised performance and scales production smoothly. Shares of NVIDIA have risen around 21.3% year to date, underperforming the Zacks Computer and Technology sector's gain of 23.4%. From a valuation standpoint, NVDA trades at a forward price-to-earnings ratio of 16.60, below the sector's average of 20.93. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for NVIDIA's fiscal 2027 and 2028 earnings implies a year-over-year increase of approximately 93.9% and 68%, respectively. On October 8, the Financial Times reported that OpenAI's annualized revenue was about $50 billion, roughly $20 billion below figures widely reported in September. AI stocks sold off. Nvidia Corporation (NASDAQ:NVDA) dropped about 3%, erasing roughly $170 billion in value, while Broadcom Inc. (NASDAQ:AVGO) fell more than 4%. Just hours later, Bloomberg reported that OpenAI expects to reach or exceed $70 billion in annualized revenue by year-end. The gap came down to how revenue was counted. The higher figure includes sales through OpenAI's cloud partners, which OpenAI's own number leaves out. Bloomberg's report suggests OpenAI could reach $70 billion in annualized revenue by year-end, although achieving that target would require substantial growth from September's $50 billion run rate. If the market overreacted to OpenAI's revenue figures, the selloff may have created buying opportunities. These AI stocks may deserve a closer look. Nvidia sells to nearly every major AI lab and cloud provider, so one company's revenue figure says little about its overall demand. Jensen Huang said last month that Nvidia expects to double the number of chips it sells in 2027, and management has guided to about 70% revenue growth in fiscal 2028. The company also added a record $150 billion to its buyback, a strong sign of confidence in its cash flow. ​The valuation makes the selloff even harder to justify. The forward non-GAAP P/E of 25.50x sits about 40% below its 5-year average of 42.15x. Similarly, the forward Price-to-sales ratio of 13.93x is 29% below its average of 19.67x. So even while sitting at the center of the AI boom, Nvidia's stock trades at a considerable discount. The EPS outlook is solid. Analysts expect earnings to grow 95% this fiscal year and 71% the next. Based on fiscal 2028 earnings, the P/E falls to about 15x.Nvidia held approximately $23.2 billion in net cash, including marketable debt securities, as of July 26, 2026. The stock's valuation may look more attractive than the recent sell-off suggests, but it's not the only stock near record levels that Wall Street is watching. See the 10 best stocks near all-time highs to buy, with NVDA ranked No. 1. Broadcom's link to OpenAI is more direct. It's building OpenAI's custom AI chips under a 10-gigawatt deal. The night before, the Wall Street Journal reported that the company was working to arrange more than $50 billion in financing tied to that work. Talks were described as early, and Bloomberg's account put the debt at about $30 billion for the next phase. Landing a day ahead of the OpenAI revenue headline, the report made the risk look bigger. Even so, the financing is still in early talks, and the $70 billion is a projection, not cash in hand. The chip rollout extends through 2029, meaning OpenAI's growth must continue well beyond this year. Broadcom's forward non-GAAP P/E of 32.30x sits about 18% above its 5-year average of 27.34x. Its forward Price-to-sales ratio of 16.96x is roughly 30% above its average of 13.06x. The EPS outlook helps justify the premium. Analysts expect earnings to grow 71% this fiscal year and 66% the next. Based on fiscal 2027 earnings, the P/E drops to about 19x. Broadcom ranked No. 6 on our list of the 10 Best Pick and Shovel AI Stocks to Buy for the Long Term. See which five stocks ranked higher. The risk for investors is concentration. If OpenAI falls short, Broadcom will feel it more than Nvidia.​ Hedge funds had been adding to Nvidia. The number of funds holding it rose from 275 in Q1 to 285 in Q2, and stakes grew from $83.9 billion to $94.7 billion. Broadcom's fund count slipped from 173 to 170, and stakes fell from $32.8 billion to $29.1 billion.​ I think investors who sold these two on the OpenAI headline sold for the wrong reason. The selloff treated an accounting difference like a drop in demand, even though OpenAI still expects to hit $70 billion by year-end, a target that remains uncertain. For those looking to buy the dip, Nvidia looks like the safer option, while Broadcom offers more upside potential but also greater risk, if OpenAI delivers. While we acknowledge the risk and potential of NVDA as an investment, our conviction lies in the belief that some AI stocks hold greater promise for delivering higher returns and doing so within a shorter time frame.
